Answers start with the short version and link to deeper guides. Industrial real estate is property built to make, store, move, or service goods, including warehouses, distribution centers, manufacturing plants, flex buildings, and outdoor storage yards. Most industrial leases are net: tenants pay base rent plus their share of taxes, insurance, and common-area costs. Value follows documented income, building function (clear height, docks, truck court, power), and location, not price per square foot alone. In Illinois, property taxes are often the largest operating expense; Cook County assesses industrial property differently from the collar counties. Chicagoland’s rail, interstate, and air connections make it one of North America’s largest and most liquid industrial markets. h: What is flex space?
t: Flex combines finished office or showroom space (often a quarter or more) with warehouse, lab or light assembly space. Usually lower and with more grade-level doors than a warehouse, it suits companies needing offices and goods together. See flex space in the glossary .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is small-bay industrial?
t: Small-bay (or shallow-bay) buildings have suites of a few thousand to roughly 25,000 square feet for contractors, service businesses, distributors and light manufacturers. Suites typically include an office, drive-in or dock door and separate utilities. Limited new construction supports a deep local market for 10,000 to 100,000 SF properties.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is a last-mile industrial facility?
t: A last-mile (or last-touch) warehouse or service building serves final deliveries near dense population. Customer, labor and arterial road access, plus van and fleet parking, outweigh size or height. Chicago and inner-ring suburban infill sites are typical locations.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is industrial outdoor storage (IOS)?
t: IOS land provides truck and trailer parking, equipment staging or material storage, usually fenced, lit, paved or graveled with little or no building. Value depends on zoning, access, surfacing, stormwater compliance and scarcity; many municipalities restrict it. See IOS in the glossary .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is cold storage, and why is it different?
t: Cold storage is a temperature-controlled warehouse for refrigerated or frozen goods. Insulated panels, refrigeration systems, freezer-grade floors with under-slab heating, heavy power, and specialized docks make it far more expensive to build and convert than a dry warehouse. That cost, plus food-safety requirements, keeps supply limited and tenants sticky.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What do Class A, B, and C mean for industrial buildings?
t: Class describes age and functionality: A is newer, with modern clear heights, ESFR sprinklers, deep truck courts and wide columns; B is older but functional; C has limits such as low clear height, tight columns or poor access. Classes are not standardized; compare specifications. See industrial building classes .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: Who leases and owns industrial buildings?
t: Tenants include manufacturers, distributors, third-party logistics (3PL), e-commerce and retail companies, contractors, food and beverage firms and service businesses. Owners include occupying owner-users, private investors, family offices, syndicators, private equity funds, institutions and publicly traded REITs. Owner-users and private investors are the most common 10,000 to 100,000 SF buyers.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is a truck court, and how deep should it be?
t: The truck court is the paved maneuvering and parking area before dock doors. Modern single-sided courts commonly measure 120 to 135 feet, with more depth needed when trucks use both sides. Shallow courts limit truck access and are hard to fix. See truck court . These are screening examples, not safe-clearance guarantees. Review the sourced vehicle dimensions and turning-path reference and have a qualified engineer check the fleet's entry, backing, and exit paths.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: Why does column spacing matter in an industrial building?
t: Column spacing affects how efficiently racking, aisles, and equipment fit. Wider spacing adds flexibility; tight spacing wastes floor area and may rule out users. Modern buildings commonly use 50-foot bays with deeper speed bays at docks. See column spacing .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is an ESFR sprinkler system?
t: ESFR (early suppression, fast response) is a ceiling sprinkler system designed to suppress high-piled storage fires without in-rack sprinklers in many configurations. Adequacy depends on commodity, storage and building height, and water supply; a fire-protection engineer should confirm fit for each tenant. See ESFR sprinklers .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How much electrical power does an industrial building need?
t: Lighting and battery charging may need modest service; manufacturing, cold storage, and EV fleets may need much more. Service is described by amperage, voltage, and phase; three-phase is standard for motors and machinery. Confirm capacity with an electrician and utility, as upgrades can take months. See three-phase power .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What should I know about the floor slab?
t: Racking, forklifts and machinery depend on slab thickness, reinforcement, capacity and flatness. Tall racks and narrow-aisle equipment need level floors; heavy manufacturing needs high capacity. Review drawings, cracking and joint failure; have an engineer assess demanding uses. See slab load and flatness .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How much office space is typical in an industrial building?
t: Warehouse and distribution buildings often have under 10 to 15 percent office; flex buildings may have more. Excess office raises costs, may sit empty, and narrows the tenant pool. Match office area to local users. See office finish percentage .

h: How long are industrial leases?
t: Industrial leases commonly run three to ten years: often three to five for small-bay and small-business tenants, ten or more for large distribution and build-to-suit. Longer terms usually bring more landlord-funded improvements and free rent; shorter terms offer flexibility. Renewal options let tenants extend.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How do rent escalations work in industrial leases?
t: Base rent usually rises by a fixed percentage or amount per square foot; some leases use CPI or stepped increases. Escalations compound, so model total rent over the term. See escalations .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is a tenant improvement (TI) allowance?
t: A TI allowance funds tenant build-out or modifications such as offices, electrical, lighting, restrooms, or dock work. Usually quoted per square foot, it reflects lease term and credit and is recovered through rent. Clarify construction management and treatment of unused funds. See TI allowance .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How is industrial rent quoted?
t: Industrial rent is usually annual dollars per square foot, net of taxes, insurance and CAM. Smaller suites may quote monthly gross rent. Confirm net or gross, annual or monthly, and request current expense estimates.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: Who pays for the roof, HVAC, and structural repairs in an industrial lease?
t: The lease controls. Tenants commonly maintain their space and HVAC; landlords retain roof replacement and structure. Some “absolute NNN” leases shift everything to tenants. Distinguish repair and replacement duties and whether replacements can be amortized into CAM.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What should I ask before leasing a warehouse?
t: Confirm zoning allows your use; clear height, door types and count, truck-court depth, and trailer parking; electrical service; sprinkler adequacy for your storage; office and restroom count; current taxes, insurance, and CAM; repair and replacement responsibilities; renewal and expansion rights; restoration obligations at move-out; and access hours, security, and outdoor storage rights. The tour checklist covers what to measure.

h: Should a business lease or buy its industrial building?
t: Buying offers control, equity, rent-increase protection and a long-term asset, but ties up capital and adds concentration and repair risk. Leasing preserves cash and flexibility. p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is a build-to-suit?
t: A build-to-suit serves a specific tenant or buyer, usually committed before construction. A long lease or purchase commitment secures needed specifications and reduces developer leasing risk. Site selection, entitlements, design and construction often take a year or more.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is a speculative (spec) industrial building?
t: A speculative (spec) building anticipates demand without a signed tenant. Generic modern standards suit many users and permit faster occupancy than build-to-suit, while added supply can affect submarket rents.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is an industrial sublease, and is it a good option?
t: A sublease offers some or all of a tenant's space, usually with landlord consent. It may cost less and include furniture or racking, but cannot exceed the original term and depends on the tenant's good standing. Read the master lease.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What security deposit or guaranty will an industrial landlord ask for?
t: Security reflects tenant finances, time in business, lease term, and landlord costs for improvements and commissions. Expect a cash deposit or letter of credit; newer or smaller tenants may also need a personal or corporate guaranty. Negotiate a burn-down after on-time payments.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: Who pays the broker on an industrial lease?
t: Landlords usually pay leasing commissions under their listing agreement, typically sharing them with the tenant's broker. Arrangements vary; confirm each broker's compensation and required Illinois agency disclosures. See leasing commission .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is a letter of intent (LOI) in commercial real estate?
t: An LOI summarizes price or rent, term, contingencies, timing and conditions before the purchase agreement or lease. Business terms usually do not bind, but confidentiality or exclusivity may. Clear terms reduce surprises. See LOI .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is an industrial REIT?
t: An industrial REIT owns and usually operates industrial properties, distributing most taxable income. Public REITs offer liquidity and diversification, but no individual building control; share prices move with the market. Direct ownership offers control and tax-planning options with less liquidity.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What do core, value-add, and opportunistic mean?
t: They describe risk strategies. Core is stabilized, well-located property with long leases and low leverage. Core-plus adds modest upside. Value-add involves leasing up vacancy, renovating, or re-tenanting to raise income. Opportunistic includes development, heavy repositioning, or distressed situations with the highest risk and expected return. See value-add vs. core .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is the difference between an owner-user and an investor buyer?
t: Owner-users buy for occupancy, location, layout and control; investors buy tenant income. Owner-users may pay more for vacant or soon-vacant buildings, especially with SBA 504 financing; investors pay for existing leases. The fitting buyer pool shapes pricing and marketing. See owner-user vs. investor .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is a 1031 exchange, and how does it work for industrial property?
t: A Section 1031 exchange can defer federal capital gains tax when proceeds from an investment property sale are reinvested in another qualifying property. IRS rules generally require identification within 45 days and acquisition within 180 days, with proceeds held by a qualified intermediary. Industrial property may be exchanged for other real property held for investment or business use. Consult a tax advisor. See 1031 exchange .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is a sale-leaseback?
t: A business sells its occupied building to an investor and simultaneously leases it back long term. Equity becomes working capital without moving operations; the buyer gets a known tenant. Rent and lease terms drive price. See the selling guide’s sale-leaseback section .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How do you finance an industrial property purchase?
t: Sources include banks, credit unions, life companies, CMBS lenders, debt funds, and SBA 504 or 7(a) loans for owner-users. Lenders test LTV, debt-service coverage, and sometimes debt yield, as well as lease term, tenant credit, and environmental reports. Compare rate, term, amortization, recourse, reserves, and prepayment terms. See financing in the investment guide .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How useful is price per square foot for industrial property?
t: Price per square foot helps compare owner-user and vacant buildings but hides differences in land, clear height, office, yard, condition, and lease terms. Use it with income value and replacement cost, comparing similar buildings in the same submarket and size range.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What is WALT, and why does it matter?
t: WALT is remaining lease term weighted by rent or square footage. Longer WALT supports predictable income and financing; shorter WALT adds rollover risk but may let rents reset to market. See WALT .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What are DSCR and LTV?
t: DSCR (debt service coverage ratio) divides NOI by annual loan payments; lenders commonly require above 1.0, often 1.25 or higher. LTV (loan-to-value) divides loan amount by property value. The lower loan allowed by these tests usually controls. See DSCR and LTV .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: What are IRR, equity multiple, and cash-on-cash return?
t: Cash-on-cash is annual pre-tax cash flow divided by equity invested. Equity multiple is total cash returned divided by equity over the hold. IRR annualizes returns based on the timing of all cash flows, including sale proceeds. Each measures something different. See IRR .

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How do you determine market rent for an industrial building?
t: Market rent comes from signed leases for comparable space (size, location, clear height, doors, office, and condition), adjusted for free rent and improvement allowances. Asking rents show expectations, not deals. Ask brokers or appraisers for lease comparables.

p: Industrial real estate FAQ: 100 common questions, answered
h: How do interest rates affect industrial property values?
t: Higher rates raise borrowing costs and required returns, tending to raise cap rates and lower prices unless rent growth offsets them. Lower rates generally reverse this. h: Specifications explained and why each matters
t: Explain each specification's practical effect and separate measured facts from assumptions or broker shorthand. Clear height Clear height is usually measured from the finished floor to the lowest obstruction, not the roof deck. It affects racking, equipment, lighting, and sprinklers; check beams, joists, ducts, heaters, fans, and piping. Column spacing and speed bays Spacing affects storage, forklift movement, production cells, and demising. Speed bays can add dock staging depth; verify dimensions and obstructions. Dock-high doors and door ratio Dock-high loading supports trailer-height movement, often critical for distribution. Door-to-area ratios compare loading intensity, but the right ratio depends on operations, trailer dwell, staffing, and scheduling. Drive-in doors These admit vehicles, equipment, or vans at grade. Dock levelers, seals, shelters, and bumpers These affect safety, weather protection, handling, and efficiency. Review condition, capacity, controls, and maintenance records. p: Industrial building types and specifications
h: Class A, B, and C as informal labels
t: Class labels are market shorthand, not an official standard. Tie them to inspectable, documented facts. Informal ways people describe industrial building class Label Common description Caution Class A Newer or recently modernized building with stronger loading, height, systems, truck circulation, life-safety features, and institutional-quality records. A small Class A building may still be wrong for a user if doors, power, or zoning do not fit. Class B Functional building with some older features, moderate office finish, usable loading, and a condition profile that may require selective capital work. Class B can be a broad category, so list the actual strengths and weaknesses. Class C Older or more specialized building with lower clear height, limited loading, heavier deferred maintenance, or narrower reuse. Class C does not mean unusable; it means the buyer pool may be more specific and diligence may be more important.

p: Industrial building types and specifications
h: How specs translate to buyer and tenant pools
t: Specifications determine who can operate efficiently. Strong doors, turning, power, and fire protection may broaden distribution or manufacturing demand compared with a similarly sized building with limited utility. Functional obsolescence is a mismatch with current operating needs, such as low clear height, shallow truck courts, insufficient power, limited parking, excess office finish, difficult column spacing, or loading unsuited to building size. Investors assess re-tenanting risk by estimating the potential user pool, improvement timing, and required capital. See the investment diligence guide and commercial leasing guide . Broader pool: flexible layout, adequate power, code-compliant improvements, documented systems, and common loading patterns. Narrower pool: very specialized equipment, unusual floor plan, unresolved environmental history, nonconforming yard, or limited truck access. Seller takeaway: disclose constraints clearly and support strengths with records rather than adjectives.

p: Truck dimensions and turning paths
h: Turning circle, swept path, and offtracking
t: Turning circle diameter vs. radius Diameter spans a circle; radius is half only when both use the same circle and measurement convention. A curb-to-curb wheel path is not a wall-to-wall body envelope. Ask which reference point, steering lock, speed, and maneuver were measured. Swept path and outer sweep A swept path is the area a vehicle occupies during a maneuver. Its outer boundary includes front corners, mirrors, body overhang, and trailer swing, not just tire tracks. Offtracking Rear wheels and a trailer do not follow the tractor's front-wheel path in a low-speed turn; they commonly track inward. Trailer length, wheelbase, axle locations, articulation, steering, and approach angle change the path. Design vehicle AASHTO labels such as WB-62 and WB-67 describe specific geometric templates, not interchangeable fleet measurements or a universal radius. A qualified engineer must select a current design vehicle and compare it with the site's fleet and maneuvers. Cited fleet specifications do not establish a complete configuration’s turning radius, so none is given. Forward circulation, dock backing, opposing traffic and queuing require different checks. FHWA road-size limits are not turning templates.

h: Site-review checklist

Survey the constraints: gate openings, curb returns, driveways, dock angles, court depth, grade changes, fences, bollards, poles, parked vehicles, easements, fire access, snow storage, and overhead obstructions. Test the maneuver: have a qualified civil/transportation engineer perform fleet-specific swept-path analysis for entry, turns, backing, unloading, and exit, including required operational margins and conflicts. Check access and operation: local truck routes, bridge/underpass restrictions, delivery rules, pavement capacity, loading equipment, and municipal approvals. Legal road width or nominal cargo size is not a guaranteed safe clearance. Also use the building evaluation checklist , building specifications and industrial due-diligence guide .

t: A Phase II may sample soil, groundwater, soil gas, indoor air, or other media to test specific concerns. It cannot prove that no risk exists anywhere on the property. Qualified environmental professionals should address sampling methods, seasonal conditions, building pressure, and mitigation design.

t: Older industrial buildings may need separate surveys for asbestos, lead paint, PCBs in equipment or caulk, underground and aboveground tanks, hydraulic lifts, sumps, and floor drains. t: Title and survey connect legal rights to physical use. The title commitment lists requirements and exceptions; the ALTA survey shows boundaries, easements, improvements, access, and encroachments. Review access rights, shared drives, cross-parking, utilities, drainage easements, signage, covenants, and reciprocal easements. A truck entrance across another parcel needs documented rights, not just historical use. For rail-served property, confirm agreements, switch rights, track maintenance, active service, clearance, and who controls access. Rail value depends on legal and physical service rights matching the marketing description.

t: Confirm zoning district, permitted and special uses, variances, nonconforming rights, outdoor storage, parking, truck routing, screening, signage, and hours. Check open permits, violations, expired approvals, fire-code issues, unpermitted mezzanines, and tenant improvements needing closeout. h: Operational and lease diligence for leased industrial
t: Verify rent-roll income, obligations, and operating rights against signed documents. Request every lease, amendment, guaranty, side letter, estoppel, SNDA, and occupancy notice. Estoppels: confirm rent, term, deposits, defaults, options, exclusive rights, and tenant claims. SNDAs: coordinate lender, buyer, and tenant rights after a foreclosure or ownership change. CAM reconciliations: test recoveries, caps, exclusions, reserves, management fees, and year-end balances. Repair obligations: identify who pays for roof, structure, HVAC, pavement, dock equipment, fire protection, and capital replacements. Hazardous materials clauses: compare lease rights to actual operations, permits, storage, and environmental reports. Parking and trailer rights: confirm allocated spaces, yard rights, storage limits, and rules for containers or fleet vehicles. The commercial leasing guide explains why lease labels do not replace a clause-by-clause review.

p: Industrial property due diligence: physical and environmental
h: Utilities and infrastructure
t: Compare electricity, gas, water, sanitary and storm sewer, compressed air, fiber, and telecom with the user's equipment and occupancy schedule before commitment. Electrical capacity may involve ComEd , the serving utility, an electrical engineer, and the equipment vendor. Confirm voltage, phase, amperage, transformer ownership, spare capacity, upgrade lead times, and shutdown requirements. For existing or proposed battery energy storage, collect ownership and service contracts, approved plans, utility permissions, commissioning records, safety documentation and removal obligations. The BESS owner guide explains storage, peak savings, engineered backup, fire and insurance review, and standalone storage land leases. Neither a large service nor nearby transmission guarantees interconnection capacity. For gas, water, and sewer, check meter size, pressure, discharge limits, floor drains, pretreatment, process water, fire flow, and municipal capacity. General serviceability does not confirm fiber or telecom.

Buyers should distinguish routine maintenance from issues affecting value, financing, insurability, or lawful use. Support material findings with report pages, photos, contractor proposals, municipal responses, title exceptions, lease clauses, or consultant memos.

p: Property taxes on Illinois industrial real estate
h: How Illinois property tax works at a high level
t: Illinois industrial property taxes are local, within a state-supervised system: assessment, equalization, levy, rate, bill, and collection. Check each step against the parcel’s county, municipality, school district, and special districts. From assessment to bill Assessment The assessor estimates taxable value. Outside Cook County, Illinois generally assesses at 33⅓% of fair cash value before equalization and exemptions; Cook County uses its own classification levels. Equalization An equalization factor, or multiplier, may adjust assessments for greater uniformity. See assessed value and equalization factor . Levy Taxing districts set levies for schools, municipalities, counties, parks, libraries, fire, sanitary, and other local services. Rate and extension The county clerk extends rates against equalized assessed value; the assessor does not set the rate. Bill and collection The county treasurer bills and collects. Illinois taxes are commonly paid in installments after the tax year; confirm dates with the county treasurer.

p: Retirement planning with commercial real estate
h: Can rental income or a building sale fund retirement plan contributions?
t: Ordinary rent generally is not IRA compensation or self employed plan earned income. Sale proceeds, appreciation, cash and real estate professional status alone do not establish qualifying compensation. Eligible wages or self employment earnings, including some active real estate business income, may support contributions; sufficient joint filer compensation may permit spousal IRAs. Have a CPA classify activity, payroll and entity income, not relabel rent or invent fees. For eligibility, deductions and limits, see IRS Publication 590-A and Publication 560 . Contributions, transfers, rollovers and conversions are different Transfers and rollovers move eligible retirement assets, unlike annual contributions. Check distribution permission, receiving account acceptance, withholding and deadlines; coordinate providers directly to avoid personal receipt. IRA rollover frequency rules vary by transfer type; RMDs cannot be rolled over. Roth conversions can create taxable income; illiquid property needs supported valuation and tax cash. You cannot sell personal property to your IRA or contribute it ordinarily. Seek advice before contracts or title transfers.

p: Retirement planning with commercial real estate
h: What personal use and related party transactions are prohibited?
t: IRA property is not for personal or business use. Prohibited transactions cover improper use and disqualified persons: owners, certain fiduciaries, spouses, ancestors, lineal descendants and their spouses, and certain controlled entities. Relatives' status varies; indirect personal benefit can still violate rules. p: Battery energy storage systems: an industrial owner's guide
h: What is the difference between kW, kWh and storage duration?
t: kW measures delivery rate; kWh measures energy. Power alone does not establish duration. At larger scales, 1 MW equals 1,000 kW and 1 MWh equals 1,000 kWh. Illustration: 1,000 kWh of delivered energy at a constant 250 kW lasts four hours ideally. With only 800 kWh available after reserves and capacity limits, duration is 3.2 hours before any losses outside that measurement boundary. Actual runtime varies; usable battery DC energy is not the same as delivered AC energy. Specify nominal and usable capacity, beginning and end of life, and measurement at cells, inverter or meter. Account for temperature, HVAC and control loads, efficiency, cycling, standby time, reserves and degradation. Temperature, equipment ratings and state of charge can also limit power. Round trip efficiency compares returned and charging energy at defined boundaries; batteries return less than they take in. Aging and cycling generally reduce capacity. Warranties can limit years, throughput, cycles, temperature and operating conditions. Replacement or augmentation may require approvals, downtime and disposal planning.

p: How is net operating income calculated for commercial property?
h: What is NOI, and what is included?
t: Net operating income = effective gross income (EGI) minus operating expenses. Start with full-occupancy rent on the chosen lease or market basis, less vacancy, free rent and collection losses, plus other property income and recoveries. Reconcile rent roll, signed amendments, receivables and ledger. Typical expenses are real estate taxes, building insurance, owner-paid utilities, repairs, maintenance, contracted services and management. When comparing professionally managed investments, include a supported management allowance even if the owner self-manages. Owner business revenue, tenant sales, refundable deposits and loan proceeds are not property rental income. NOI usually excludes mortgage principal and interest, depreciation, owner income taxes, acquisition costs, tenant improvements, leasing commissions and major capital replacements. Replacement reserves may sit below NOI or enter a lender-adjusted measure. State and reconcile the convention; do not compare incompatible figures.

t: Separate trailing-12-month results, a forward annual estimate and stabilized NOI. Buyers may remove one-time income, replace related-party service costs with supported costs, normalize maintenance, adjust management fees, budget insurance renewal and test future Illinois taxes. No adjustment is automatic; retain its evidence and effective date. After lease expiry, model downtime, tenant improvements and commissions. p: DCF explained for commercial real estate owners
h: How do you build a property cash-flow projection?
t: Set valuation date and hold period. Project tenant rent, options and expirations; separate recoveries, taxes, insurance, repairs and management. Model rollover retention or vacancy, downtime, free rent, supported new rent, tenant improvements (TI) and leasing commissions (LC). Do not count the same vacancy loss in reduced rent and a separate deduction. Property cash flow is more than NOI : subtract capital replacements and leasing costs when incurred, and state reserve treatment. In a 10,000-100,000-SF building, one tenant departure or roof project can dominate a year. Use condition reports and lease abstracts, not a universal rent-growth rate. Unlevered cash flow excludes financing. Equity models add acquisition loan proceeds, subtract hold-period debt service and deduct sale payoff and finance charges. Match discount rates and return labels to cash flows; separate pre-tax and after-tax models.

p: DCF explained for commercial real estate owners
h: Discount rate versus cap rate: what is the difference?
t: Discount rates value future cash today at an assumed required return. Cap rates divide one year’s income by value. Exit caps assume resale, commonly using next-year stabilized NOI at hold’s end. These rates are neither interchangeable nor necessarily equal. For end-of-year cash flow, present value = cash flow / (1 + discount rate) year . Net present value (NPV) subtracts the initial investment from discounted receipts. Positive NPV means the modeled investment exceeds the chosen return requirement on these assumptions, not that the outcome is certain. IRR is the rate that makes NPV zero. Later negative outlays can produce multiple or unhelpful IRRs; dated cash flows also differ from simple annual periods. Keep NPV, required capital and downside exposure visible even when IRR looks attractive.

p: DCF explained for commercial real estate owners
h: DCF worked example: operating cash, reversion and present value
t: Illustration only, not market data, an appraisal or an investment recommendation. Assumptions: three-year unlevered hold, end-of-year receipts, no income taxes and an 8% discount rate. Assumed annual dollars; capital and leasing cash outlays below NOI Year NOI Capital / TI / LC Operating cash 1 $200,000 $50,000 $150,000 2 $210,000 $30,000 $180,000 3 $220,000 $30,000 $190,000 Assume year-4 NOI of $230,000 and a 7% exit cap. Gross year-3 reversion = $230,000 / 0.07 = $3,285,714.29; after assumed 2% sale costs, net reversion is $3,220,000. Year-3 total cash is $3,410,000, including $190,000 operating cash. Year-4 NOI prices the sale but is not received again during the hold. Present value = $150,000 / 1.08 + $180,000 / 1.08 2 + $3,410,000 / 1.08 3 = $3,000,177.82 . With $3,000,000 all-in initial investment, NPV is $177.82; at $3,100,000, NPV is negative $99,822.18. Results depend entirely on assumptions and cash timing.

p: DCF explained for commercial real estate owners
h: How do exit cap, rent and downtime change the result?
t: At $230,000 year-4 NOI, illustrative gross resale is $3,833,333 at a 6% exit cap, $3,285,714 at 7% and $2,875,000 at 8%, rounded to dollars before sale costs. A higher exit cap lowers resale at the same income. None is a Chicago market claim. Model discount/exit-rate combinations and a separate operating downside: lower collected rent, higher tax and insurance, longer downtime, larger TI/LC, capital overruns and delayed sale. Rent growth and a lower exit cap are not guaranteed benefits. In a levered case, include refinancing maturity and required additional equity, not just revised return. Direct capitalization is a useful NOI/cap-rate snapshot for stabilized income. DCF exposes changes and execution costs, but detail cannot make speculative assumptions reliable. Have an appraiser and financial/tax advisers review property-specific inputs and conventions.

p: DCF explained for commercial real estate owners
h: Owner questions and answers
t: Is the discount rate the same as the cap rate? No. A discount rate values a series of future cash flows; a cap rate relates one year of NOI to value. An exit cap rate is a future resale assumption. Does a high IRR prove a good real estate investment? No. Cash timing and assumptions drive IRR; nonconventional flows can mislead. It does not measure absolute capital at risk. Review NPV, required equity and downside. Should DCF include mortgage payments? Include debt service and loan payoff in a levered equity model, not in an unlevered property model. Match the discount rate to the cash-flow basis.

p: Free commercial property DCF and investment calculator
h: What formulas does this DCF calculator use?
t: Effective gross income (EGI) = scheduled rent - vacancy/credit loss + percentage rent + other income + recoveries. Standard NOI = EGI - operating expenses - management fees - property taxes - insurance. This tool's reserve-adjusted NOI also deducts the separately entered replacement reserve. Do not compare it with a reserve-free broker or lender NOI without reconciling the convention. GRM = price / annual scheduled rent. Cap rate = year-one reserve-adjusted NOI / price. Initial equity = price + closing costs - loan + upfront interest reserve. Cash-on-cash = (year-one reserve-adjusted NOI - debt service) / initial equity, before income tax and one-time capital events. Monthly payment = principal × monthly rate / [1 - (1 + monthly rate) -number of payments ]. At a zero rate, payment = principal / number of payments. Interest-only periods are in years; principal amortization begins afterward. DSCR = reserve-adjusted NOI / annual debt service. Debt yield = reserve-adjusted NOI / initial loan. LTV = loan / price. Gross sale value = annualized sale-month reserve-adjusted NOI / exit cap rate. Net sale proceeds deduct selling costs, outstanding debt and modeled exit taxes. A shortfall stays negative; a refinance or balloon payoff can also require extra cash. Total equity cash flow = reserve-adjusted NOI - TI - LC - additional capex - debt service + reserve draw + gross refinance procee

p: How can owners reduce commercial building operating costs?
h: Which operating costs should an owner review first?
t: Collect at least a year of bills and contracts. Separate recurring expenses, one-time repairs, capital replacements and tenant payments. Compare relevant area, consumption, hours and occupancy; heated manufacturing and unheated storage costs are not comparable. See budgeting and normalized expense comparisons . Track actions, responsible parties, implementation costs, supported benefits, lease recoveries, approvals and results. Check duplicate invoices, incorrect meters, vacant-area services, expired promotions and auto-renewals. Charges are not automatically tenant-recoverable.

p: How can owners reduce commercial building operating costs?
h: How can industrial owners reduce energy and utility waste?
t: Review interval electricity, demand charges, seasonal gas, supply and delivery costs. Confirm utility tariffs; cheaper commodity quotes may hide fees or unfavorable renewals. Demand savings depend on peak timing, not annual kilowatt-hours alone. Ask qualified contractors about LEDs and controls, occupancy scheduling, office HVAC setpoints, dock seals and weather-stripping. Match controls to tasks, hours and equipment. Preserve required emergency lighting, ventilation, fire and freeze protection. Check water/sewer bills for leaks, irrigation timing, meter errors and locally permitted adjustments; sewer charges do not simply disappear. Check the official ComEd business savings portal and Nicor Gas business efficiency resources . Offers depend on account, territory, measure and current rules. Before purchase, confirm eligibility, approved equipment, preapproval, deadlines and whether landlord or tenant applies. No rebate, approval or savings percentage is promised. Simple payback = net project cost / supported annual savings. Include installation, commissioning, disruption and maintenance; count rebates only if eligible and approved. A project may lower tenant costs or improve resilience without immediately increasing owner NOI.

p: How can owners reduce commercial building operating costs?
h: Preventive maintenance versus deferred repairs
t: Track roof sections, HVAC, docks, pavement, drains and life-safety systems by condition, warranty, maintenance responsibility and next inspection. Qualified inspections can distinguish repair from replacement and schedule work around tenants. Deferring leaks or clogged drains can increase damage, not save money. Use a multi-year roof, HVAC and paving plan; compare scopes, restoration, permit responsibilities and warranties. Do not cut required fire-system testing, access, structural repairs or worker safety. Engineering and municipal requirements govern the work.

p: How can owners reduce commercial building operating costs?
h: How do service rebids and management fees reduce waste?
t: Rebid waste, landscaping, snow, janitorial, security and maintenance at identical service levels. Specify frequency, disposal fees, after-hours response, snow triggers, de-icing, insurance, reporting and escalation. A low bid may cost more if it excludes emergencies or transfers uninsured risk. Compare management fee bases and services, not percentages alone: collections, reporting, lease administration, capital supervision and extras. Check invoice approvals and related-party vendors. Calendar renewals before cancellation windows close.

p: How can owners reduce commercial building operating costs?
h: How can an owner reduce CAM disputes and improve recoveries?
t: For each lease, record pro rata share and area basis, included costs, exclusions, caps, management fees, capital-amortization permissions, gross-ups, expense stops, reconciliation deadline and audit rights. Allocate once, keep invoices, reconcile estimates to permitted actual costs, return credits and explain increases. Reduce CAM by removing waste and billing accurately, not shifting excluded costs. Caps or vacant shares may leave savings with either party. Show expense reductions and lower recoveries in the NOI bridge before claiming a benefit. Have counsel review disputed clauses and changes. For major cost categories, see the Illinois property-tax appeal and budgeting guide and insurance renewal/risk checklist ; their deadlines, evidence and trade-offs differ from vendor bids.

p: How can owners reduce commercial building operating costs?
h: A repeatable cost-control cycle
t: Record the baseline bill, service scope and owner/tenant allocation. Get comparable proposals and approvals before changing service. Track implementation cost separately from approved incentives. Compare later consumption and invoices, adjusting for weather or occupancy where relevant. Reconcile recoveries and update the next budget. Illustrative arithmetic, not a forecast: a $6,000 annual invoice reduction less $2,000 unreimbursed implementation cost yields $4,000 first-year net cash before other effects. If tenants reimburse the full recurring expense, owner NOI may not rise by $6,000.

p: How can owners reduce commercial building operating costs?
h: Owner questions and answers
t: How do I reduce CAM charges without cutting essential service? Audit scope, invoices and lease allocations; rebid comparable services and remove duplicate or ineligible charges. No. Confirm the account, measure, equipment and current program requirements, including any preapproval, before purchase or installation. Does every expense reduction increase property value? No. Lower expenses can reduce reimbursements; service cuts can worsen risk or occupancy. Calculate net owner income and capital costs first.

Replacement cost covers like-kind/quality replacement without that deduction, subject to policy terms. Land, investment value and purchase price do not set the building’s reconstruction limit. h: What belongs in a commercial operating budget?
t: Use invoices, signed leases and monthly trailing statements. Budget tenant base rent, recoveries, collection loss and ancillary income. Track taxes, insurance, utilities, repairs, snow, waste, grounds, management and recurring services; schedule renewals and seasonal bills by due date and compare annually. For Chicagoland industrial assets, review winter service and heat, roof/drains, loading equipment and paving alongside tenancy. Separate tenant-paid utilities from landlord service. Include tax notices, appeal status and insurance-renewal assumptions instead of extrapolating a quiet year. Monthly, reconcile budget and actual price, usage and timing, update collections and forecast. Tax refunds and insurance recoveries are not recurring income. NOI reconciliation preserves the operating basis; cash forecasts show liquidity timing.

h: How do I benchmark operating expenses without misleading comparisons?
t: Define whether cost per square foot uses rentable, occupied or gross area. Compare property type, heated area, tenant use, service level, period and gross/net lease basis. Separate capital and one-time costs. Utility use per operating hour or occupied area may reveal more than dollars alone. Use normalized history, comparable vendor scopes and verified peer data. This guide provides no Chicago expense ratios or market rates. A low ratio may reflect deferred maintenance, tenant-paid costs or missing management fees, not efficiency. Label sources and adjustments.

h: How much reserve cash does a commercial owner need?
t: No universal reserve percentage suffices. Schedule condition, timing, installed replacement estimates, lease responsibility and contingencies, plus vacancy carry, TI/LC, deductibles, tax timing and loan maturity. Separate lender-restricted reserves from readily available cash. Illustrative arithmetic, not a reserve recommendation: a supported $120,000 project estimate, $20,000 already dedicated and five years to completion imply $20,000 annual straight-line funding before inflation, interest or contingencies. An earlier failure requires cash sooner. Do not count both annual contributions and the eventual project as expenses in the same cash-flow model.

p: How to budget expenses, reserves and capital for a commercial building
h: Depreciation, cost segregation and 1031: what should I ask my CPA?
t: Depreciation allocates eligible capital basis over its recovery period; it is not current-year cash spending and is excluded from ordinary property NOI. Land is not depreciable. Basis allocation, placed-in-service dates, classification, elections and current law matter. See IRS Publication 946 , not a promised deduction. A cost-segregation study identifies supported components and tax classifications/recovery periods; it is neither an automatic percentage write-off nor an operating expense. Ask about study quality, basis reconciliation, timing, costs and recapture on sale. The IRS audit-guide directory links the Cost Segregation guide and warns that law may change after publication. Section 1031 may defer, not erase, qualifying gain on business/investment real-property exchanges. Property held primarily for sale does not qualify; cash or other non-like-kind property may create taxable gain. Before closing, discuss ownership, qualified-intermediary arrangements, identification and completion deadlines, debt and state taxes. See sale/1031 preparation and the IRS real-estate exchange overview . Consult a CPA and attorney; no tax result is promised.

h: Refinancing and debt costs belong in the liquidity plan
t: Track interest, amortization, fees, escrows, covenants, maturity, recourse and prepayment. DSCR compares a lender-defined income measure with debt service; LTV compares debt with its value basis; debt yield compares defined NOI with loan balance. No universal qualifying threshold applies. Refinancing plans do not erase balloon balances. Test lower proceeds, higher borrowing costs and delayed closing; calculate cash gaps after payoff and fees. Use the debt-service calculator and financing guide and levered versus unlevered projections , not a duplicate calculator.

p: Comparing commercial leases in Chicago
h: Gross and net are labels, not complete budgets
t: Gross lease Usually bundles some building expenses into rent; utilities, increases, exclusions and other charges may remain separate. Modified gross lease Allocates expenses by agreement. Confirm what is included and what can change. Net or triple-net (NNN) lease Adds taxes, insurance and maintenance to base rent, commonly. The label does not assign roof, structure, capital repairs or every operating cost. Common area maintenance (CAM) Shared property costs; review the lease’s definition, allocation, exclusions, reconciliation and review rights. Confirm whether the quoted rate is annual or monthly, its area basis and currency. Request the expense estimate and supporting history; actual pass-throughs may differ at reconciliation.

p: Comparing commercial leases in Chicago
h: Build a total occupancy-cost comparison
t: Separate recurring, upfront, refundable-security and later capital costs. Compare options over the same lease term and area basis, including scheduled increases. Recurring: base rent, tax and insurance pass-throughs, CAM, utilities, maintenance contracts, parking and other required charges. Upfront: professional review, permits, buildout, equipment installation, relocation and costs not reimbursed by a tenant-improvement allowance. Cash tied up: security deposits, prepaid rent and letters of credit. Refundable security ties up liquidity but is not automatically an operating expense. Contingent: expense increases, tenant-assigned major repairs, delayed delivery, exit restoration and costs of changing operations. Illustrative arithmetic only, not Chicago market data. If 10,000 rentable square feet were quoted at $12 per square foot per year in base rent and $4 in estimated annual pass-throughs, those two components would total $160,000 per year, or about $13,333 per month. Utilities, improvements, other charges, and future changes would still need to be added. This example is not an available property or a rent estimate. Ask for each figure’s basis. Label unknowns as estimates and test a higher-cost case rather than treating them as zero.

h: A lease-review checklist
t: Premises and use: verify the space, shared areas, permitted use, parking, loading, yard rights and operating restrictions. Term and delivery: distinguish possession, rent commencement, substantial completion and conditions to operate. Improvements: document scope, approvals, allowance, reimbursement conditions, overruns, ownership and removal obligations. Repairs: allocate ordinary maintenance and major HVAC, roof, structural, pavement and fire-protection work. Expenses: review allocation percentages, exclusions, negotiated caps, reconciliation and document-review rights. Risk: have counsel review insurance, indemnity, casualty, condemnation, default remedies and any personal guaranty. Flexibility: check renewal options and notice deadlines, assignment, subleasing, expansion, termination and restoration. An LOI organizes negotiations; wording and circumstances determine binding effect. Obtain counsel review before signing, rather than assuming all terms are nonbinding.

t: Check zoning and building requirements before setting a move-in date; allow for design, permits, utilities, construction, inspections and equipment commissioning. Document deliverables, responsible parties, completion evidence and delay consequences. Confirm timing with authorities and contractors; “available now” does not mean business-ready.

p: Researching Chicago commercial real estate
h: 1. Define what the property must do
t: Record activity, occupancy date, usable area, budget and essential physical requirements, separate from preferences. For purchases, distinguish owner occupancy, rental income and redevelopment; underwriting differs. Office Consider layout, accessibility, telecommunications, commuting and adaptation costs. Retail and service space Check customer access, visibility, deliveries, permitted activity, licensing and buildout needs. Industrial and warehouse property Evaluate loading, clear height, power, circulation and operations before comparing area. See the industrial evaluation guide . Flex and mixed-use property Identify each actual use and its share. “Flex” does not establish permission for manufacturing, retail, laboratory or assembly.

p: Researching Chicago commercial real estate
h: 2. Confirm the jurisdiction and parcel
t: “Chicago area” may mean the city or wider region. Identify municipality, county, address and every property index number (PIN). Marketing addresses may cover multiple parcels; mailing addresses do not establish zoning authority. For city property, start with Chicago zoning and building resources. For suburban property, check municipal planning and building departments; for unincorporated parcels, confirm the county authority. Use the parcel’s county assessor and treasurer. Cook County records do not cover DuPage, Lake, Will, Kane or other counties. Log the source, retrieval date, parcel or address, result and open questions. Keep source documents, not just screenshots or search snippets. The nine-county Chicagoland industrial hub links planning, zoning and parcel sources for Cook, DeKalb, DuPage, Grundy, Kane, Kendall, Lake, McHenry and Will, distinguishing county and municipal authority beyond the city.

p: Researching Chicago commercial real estate
h: 3. Verify use, condition, and obligations
t: Zoning is a starting point Give the authority your zoning designation and proposed operation. Confirm approvals, special uses, parking, loading and restrictions. Existing occupancy or a prior business does not automatically permit a new operation. Building records need interpretation Review available permits and violations; have qualified advisers investigate open issues. Public records may be incomplete and do not establish roof, structural, electrical, fire-protection or other conditions. Arrange inspections suited to the property and intended use. Taxes are not a fixed listing number Match bills and assessments to the PINs and tax year. Assessed value, tax bill and market value are different. Ask a qualified tax adviser how reassessment, appeals, incentives or a use/ownership change may affect the budget; last year’s bill is not a forecast. Access and environmental questions can change the decision Check access rights, easements, drainage and flood information. Past industrial activity may warrant environmental diligence even when current use appears ordinary. The purchase-diligence guide places these checks in acquisition review.

p: Researching Chicago commercial real estate
h: 4. Put each option on the same basis
t: Area: record the source and whether it is rentable, usable, building or land area. Cost: separate price or base rent from taxes, insurance, maintenance, utilities, improvements and transaction costs. Timing: include possession, approvals, construction and equipment installation, not just closing or lease dates. Evidence: distinguish verified facts from representations and estimates. Asking terms do not prove a completed transaction or market value. Continue to comparing commercial leases for rentals or investment and purchase diligence for acquisitions.

h: Column spacing

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Drive-in door

h: Truck court

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Trailer parking
t: Outdoor spaces used to store trailers, subject to zoning, surface, screening, and lease limits.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Cross-dock
t: A building moving freight between inbound and outbound doors with little storage time.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Rail-served
t: A property with rail access or a rail spur; service, rights, and track condition still need review.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: ESFR sprinklers
t: Early Suppression Fast Response sprinklers for certain high-piled storage conditions.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Slab load and flatness
t: Slab capacity and surface tolerance, especially for heavy storage or narrow-aisle systems.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: 3-phase power
t: Industrial electrical service; verify voltage, amperage, transformer capacity, and utility supply.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Mezzanine
t: An intermediate platform or floor inside a building, subject to permits, structure, fire, and egress review.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Office finish %
t: The portion of a building improved as office space.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Flex space
t: A suite or building combining office, showroom, light industrial, storage, or service use.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: IOS (industrial outdoor storage)
t: Land for storing vehicles, equipment, materials, containers, or trailers. Permitted use depends on zoning, screening, surface, access, and environmental controls.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Class A/B/C industrial
t: Informal market labels for relative quality, age, features, location, and tenant appeal.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Land-to-building ratio
t: The relationship between site area and building area.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Site coverage
t: The portion of a parcel covered by buildings and sometimes other impervious improvements.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Infill vs. greenfield
t: Infill sites are in developed areas; greenfields are undeveloped or less-developed land.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: NNN / triple net
t: A lease where the tenant commonly pays base rent, taxes, insurance, and operating expenses.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Gross lease
t: A lease where many property expenses are included in rent.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Modified gross
t: A lease between gross and net structures, with expenses allocated by contract.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: CAM
t: Common-area charges for costs such as snow, landscaping, lighting, security, pavement, and management, subject to lease inclusions, exclusions, caps, and allocation. See CAM reconciliation and cost controls .

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Base rent
t: Stated rent before pass-through expenses, credits, abatements, or other adjustments.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Escalations
t: Scheduled rent increases or expense adjustments, fixed, percentage-based, index-based, or tied to operating costs.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: TI allowance
t: Money a landlord contributes toward approved tenant improvements.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: LC (leasing commission)
t: Compensation paid for procuring a tenant or lease renewal; model it as a leasing cash need in the hold-period DCF .

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Expense stop
t: A threshold where the landlord covers expenses up to a stated amount and the tenant pays certain increases above it.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Estoppel certificate
t: A tenant statement confirming key lease facts, defaults, deposits, options, and claims.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: SNDA
t: Subordination, non-disturbance, and attornment agreement among tenant, landlord, and lender.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Holdover
t: A tenant remaining after lease expiration, usually subject to lease consequences and remedies.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Renewal option
t: Contractual right to extend a lease if notice, timing, and default conditions are met.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: ROFR / ROFO
t: Rights of first refusal or first offer that may affect sale or leasing flexibility.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: WALT
t: Remaining lease duration weighted by rent or area.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Rent roll
t: Summary of tenants, suites, area, rent, deposits, options, and lease dates.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: EGI (effective gross income)
t: Potential rent less vacancy and credit losses, plus collectible recoveries and other property income, stated annually. See the rent-to-NOI bridge .

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: DCF (discounted cash flow)
t: Projection discounting future property or equity cash flows to a valuation date. State capital, lease rollover, and sale assumptions. DCF guide .

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: NPV (net present value)
t: Discounted future net receipts minus initial investment at a chosen rate; positive modeled NPV is not guaranteed. Worked example .

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Discount rate
t: Required return used to convert future cash to present value, matched to levered or unlevered and pre- or after-tax cash flows. Not a cap rate.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Exit cap rate
t: Future resale capitalization assumption, commonly applied to the year after the hold's NOI. A higher rate lowers indicated resale at the same NOI.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Debt yield
t: Defined annual NOI divided by loan balance; definitions and thresholds vary by lender. Financing comparison .

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Capex (capital expenditures)
t: Cash for capital improvements or replacements, generally modeled separately from property NOI. Tax capitalization is a separate analysis.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Opex (operating expenses)
t: Recurring property operating costs on the stated accounting basis, such as taxes, insurance, maintenance and management. Debt service is separate.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Replacement reserve
t: Cash earmarked for future capital needs; funding is not payment for work. State lender and model conventions to avoid double-counting.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Coinsurance
t: A policy provision tying required insurance amounts to a specified value basis and percentage; underinsurance can reduce payment. Actual wording controls. Insurance valuation .

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: BI (business income) / loss of rents
t: Insurance for qualifying income losses after a covered event, subject to triggers, time limits, and exclusions; not ordinary vacancy or tenant-default protection.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Cook County Class 6b
t: An incentive assessment classification for qualifying industrial development, rehabilitation or reutilization, subject to application, local support and compliance. Compare incentive classes .

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: NOI
t: Effective gross property income minus operating expenses, before debt service, depreciation, and major capital needs. State the reserve convention. See NOI calculation and recoveries .

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Cap rate
t: NOI divided by price or value; a shorthand income and risk measure, not a complete valuation.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Going-in vs. exit cap
t: Going-in cap rate uses current or first-year income; exit cap rate is a resale assumption.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: DSCR
t: Debt service coverage ratio compares income available for debt payments to required debt service.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: LTV
t: Loan-to-value compares loan amount to property value, purchase price, or another lender-defined base.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: IRR
t: Internal rate of return is the discount rate that makes modeled net present value zero. Nonconventional cash flows may have multiple or no useful IRRs. See DCF return measures .

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Equity multiple
t: Total cash returned divided by total equity invested.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Cash-on-cash
t: Annual cash flow compared with cash invested, often after debt service and before taxes.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Basis
t: May mean tax basis, cost basis, or an investor's all-in cost. Confirm which definition applies.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Replacement cost
t: Estimated cost to build a similar asset today.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Sale-leaseback
t: A transaction where an owner sells a property and leases it back.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Owner-user vs. investor
t: An owner-user buys to occupy; an investor buys for income, appreciation, redevelopment, or resale.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Value-add vs. core
t: Core generally means stabilized assets with lower perceived risk; value-add involves vacancy, rollover, improvements, repositioning or other execution risk.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: 1031 exchange
t: Qualifying exchange of business or investment real property that can defer gain. Deferred exchanges generally require identification within 45 days and completion by the earlier of 180 days or the relevant tax-return due date, including extensions, subject to detailed rules. See IRS Form 8824 instructions and owner tax planning . Consult a CPA or attorney before closing.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Qualified intermediary
t: A party used to facilitate a 1031 exchange and hold exchange proceeds.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: LOI
t: A letter of intent outlining business terms before a purchase agreement or lease.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: PSA
t: A purchase and sale agreement governing price, deposits, diligence, conditions, default, and closing.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Due diligence period
t: Agreed time for a buyer to inspect records, title, survey, environmental and physical condition, leases, zoning, and financing.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Earnest money
t: A buyer deposit governed by the PSA and escrow instructions.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: PIN (property index number)
t: A parcel identifier used in county tax and assessment records.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Assessed value & equalization factor
t: Assessed value is the county’s property-tax figure, distinct from its underlying market value and the bill. County or Illinois Department of Revenue equalization factors standardize assessment levels across jurisdictions. Verify figures with the assessor and treasurer.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Triennial reassessment
t: Cook County reassesses property on a three-year cycle; verify timing and notices with the county assessor.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Township assessor
t: In most Illinois counties outside Cook, elected official who sets initial property values; the county supervisor of assessments reviews and equalizes them. Contact the county office to find the right township assessor.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Transfer tax
t: A tax that may apply at state, county, or municipal levels when real estate changes ownership.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Zoning map amendment
t: A legislative change to a parcel's zoning classification.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Special use
t: A use allowed only after specific local approval, often with conditions.

p: Industrial real estate & investment glossary
h: Variance
